extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / experimental natural philosophers (chemists, microscopists) conducting and reporting laboratory observations
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and describing empirical, observational laboratory experiments (fluid/chemical phenomena, microscopic animalcula, astronomical observations) with attention to apparatus, conditions, and qualitative detail. Emphasis on reproducible steps, observation conditions (light, temperature, contact media), and vivid descriptive record.

rubrics_metrics.name: holding the plain ... in respect of the light and the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: “holding the plain where the two liquors were contiguous in a convenient position, in respect of the light and the eye, I observed it to make a strangely vivid reflection” — position the sample relative to incident light and the observer so that optical phenomena (reflections, specular effects) are visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the vessel and observer to maximize visibility of reflected light and surface phenomena; small changes in posture or angle can reveal brisker or diminished reflection. Example: hold a small phial so incident light is strongly reflected to the eye when adding another liquid.

rubrics_metrics.name: taking care that portions might not touch one another
rubrics_metrics.description: “taking care as far as we could, that they might not touch one another; by which means, the oil being transparent, and yet a little coloured, it was easy to observe, that the smaller portions of water were so near totally environed with the oil, that they were reduced into almost perfect globes.” — keep sample portions separated to observe individual shapes and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying droplets or inclusions, introduce portions so they do not coalesce; use slightly coloured transparent surrounding liquid to provide contrast and reveal shape (globes, ellipses). Avoid touching/merging droplets if the aim is to study isolated surface curvature and interface geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of controlled temperature to effect phase changes
rubrics_metrics.description: “the phial was stopped, and suffered to rest for some time in a cold place, by which means the water continuing fluid as before, the oil of aniseeds was found coagulated in a form approaching to that it had whilst in a fluid state.” — control temperature to induce coagulation/solidification and observe resulting morphology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold samples at specified temperatures (e.g., cold place) to produce solidification/coagulation and compare reflective and surface features in fluid vs coagulated states. Note differences in reflection (dull when coagulated vs fine when fluid) and in surface roughness or flaky particle formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: incremental addition and careful staging of reagents
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some distilled quicksilver being put into a small phial, and held in such a posture ... I slowly put to it some petroleum ... observed, that as this liquor covered the quicksilver, there was at the imaginary plain where they both met, a brisker reflection than the quicksilver alone had given before.” — add reagents slowly and watch interface effects as they form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce one liquid to another slowly while observing the interface; document immediate changes at the contact plane (e.g., enhancement of reflection). Record posture and timing of additions as they affect the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of vacuum / pneumatical receiver to reveal entrapped gases and bubble formation
rubrics_metrics.description: “we then transferred it into a pneumatical receiver, and having caused the air to be pumped out by degrees, we found store of bubbles appeared at the top of the liquor, and made there a copious froth...” — remove air gradually to observe gas liberation and bubble morphology in viscous fluids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a receiver and progressive evacuation to cause bubbles to form in viscous/resinous substances; observe size, colour (rainbow colours in thin films), and whether bubbles become trapped as material resolidifies. Describe film thinness, viscosity, and resulting reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: vary contiguous media to study surface figures
rubrics_metrics.description: “the surface of water may have different figures, according as it is totally encompassed with heterogeneous fluids, or, as it is only in some places contiguous to one or more of them.” — change the adjacent fluids (different oils, air) to see how surface shape and figure vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically test different surrounding liquids (oils of cloves, turpentine, aniseed oil, spirit of wine) and states (air, frozen) to record how contact and heterogeneity alter surface curvature, ellipticity, tumidity, and figuration. Note gravity/density contrasts and adhesion to vessel walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: observe and report state-dependent surface roughness and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: “when its parts were no longer agitated ... the contiguous water grew unable to inflect, or otherwise place them ... the upper surface of the oil of aniseeds ... was far from smooth, being variously asperated by many flaky particles.” — report how surfaces change (smooth vs rough) when fluidity or temperature conditions change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare surfaces when fluids are fluid, coagulated, frozen, or in contact with air; describe roughness, flakes, embossed patterns (e.g., star figures on regulus), and whether features are raised above the horizontal plane. Provide tactile or visual descriptors where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: careful sample preparation and concentration to provoke observable organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: “having put about one-third of an ounce of whole pepper in water, and it having lain about three weeks ... I discerned in it with great surprise an incredible number of little animals” — prepare and age samples (add organic matter, concentrate by evaporation) to reveal microscopic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare samples by adding particulate organic matter (pepper), allow to stand for days or weeks, add snow-water or let water evaporate to concentrate organisms. Record timing, additions, and any washing/cleaning steps (e.g., washed rainwater) that could influence origin or abundance of animalcula.

rubrics_metrics.name: use microscopy and describe morphology and motion in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive Leewenhoek passages describing multiple sorts of animalcula: body composed of globules, horns, tails, feet, motion patterns (tumbling, rotary motion), bursting on drying — use magnification to detail form and behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a microscope to observe shape (globules, oval, elongated), appendages (horns, tails, feet), motion (nimble feet, tumbling, top-like spinning), and life-cycle behaviours (bursting on drying). Provide counts (thousands per drop), relative measures (compare to cheese-mite, hair), and behavioural notes (entanglement on filaments, extension/contraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: quantify and convey scale by analogy and relative measures
rubrics_metrics.description: “I make the proportion of one of these small water-creatures to a cheese-mite, to be like that of a bee to a horse; for, the circumference of one of these little animals in water is not so large as the thickness of a hair in a cheese-mite.” — provide relative size comparisons to familiar objects to convey scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When absolute measures are impractical, give comparisons to familiar objects (cheese-mite, grain of sand, thickness of hair) and, where possible, provide counts per unit (e.g., '6000 or 8000 in a single drop'). Such analogies help readers grasp microscopic scale and abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: repeat observations across times/conditions and report variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple notes of observing phenomena at several times (e.g., satellite apparitions across months; fluids showing different figures when observed under different temperatures or after days), indicating the need to observe repeatedly and under varying conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct observations over different days, seasons, or stages (e.g., appearance/disappearance of Saturn satellites, repeated viewing of reflective effects) to determine periodicity, variability, and reproducibility. Note any periods of invisibility or condition-dependent visibility and report dates and durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: describe apparatus, provenance, and accidental discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes such as the phosphorus discovery being accidental (residue from dissolved chalk in nitrous acid) and detailed apparatus descriptions (gilt silver box, small phial, slender pipe, pneumatical receiver) — provide equipment, materials, and context for reproducibility and provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document vessel types, materials (glass, phial, receiver), source/preparation of chemicals (e.g., dissolved chalk in nitrous acid), presentation/context (gift to the Society), and any serendipitous steps that led to discovery. This supports reproducibility and helps others replicate or understand how phenomenon arose.
